practical.title: Pointers & Memory Management — Dynamic Grades Array (Intensive Lab)
practical.summary: An intensive, four-scene hands-on lab that uses a runnable C starter program to explore dynamic memory allocation with malloc, calloc, realloc and free. Observe a working program, make targeted edits, add functionality, and verify edge cases.
practical.sourceActivity: Pointers & Memory Management — Dynamic Grades Array (Intensive Lab)

coachingPrompts: What do you predict will happen before you run it?
What evidence shows that your change worked?
Can you explain the result in your own words?

teachingPlaylist.title: Observe: Run and read the starter program
teachingPlaylist.description: Run the provided program and observe how malloc, pointer variables and free are used.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Identify where memory is allocated and which variable holds the address returned by malloc.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: We will compile and run the starter program and observe prompts and final output. Notice the grades pointer and the malloc call. Predict what will happen if allocation fails.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample:
Run: gcc -std=c11 main.c -o main && printf "3
80
90
100
" | ./main -> Average grade: 90.00
teachingPlaylist.scenario: A teacher wants to enter a set of grades at runtime and compute their average without knowing the number in advance.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Run the program and explain which variable stores the heap address and where the floats are kept.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Thinking that the array elements live on the stack because we used grades[i] syntax. Actually, the memory lives on the heap.
teachingPlaylist.recap: malloc returns an address which grades stores; free returns that memory to the system.
codeSteps: Open main.c and read top-level includes and declarations.
Compile and run using the provided command.

teachingPlaylist.title: Modify: Replace malloc with calloc and initialize pointer
teachingPlaylist.description: Make two pinpointed changes to learn difference between malloc and calloc and practice pointer initialization.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Understand calloc's zero-initialization and why pointer initialization to NULL is a safe habit.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Change the declaration to initialize grades to NULL and use calloc for allocation. Recompile and observe behavior with zero inputs to confirm zero initialization.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample:
Change lines, compile and run: gcc -std=c11 main.c -o main && printf "3
0
0
0
" | ./main -> Average grade: 0.00
teachingPlaylist.scenario: A form where some values might be optional — zero-initialization can reduce chance of using garbage before deliberate assignment.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Make the two edits and run the program. Predict whether observed behavior will change when you input non-zero values.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Forgetting to check calloc's return value or forgetting to remove the cast in environments that warn (we keep the cast here for clarity).
teachingPlaylist.recap: calloc zeros memory; initialization of pointers prevents accidental use before allocation.
codeSteps: Compile and run the test command.

teachingPlaylist.title: Build: Add validation and realloc support
teachingPlaylist.description: Add grade validation and an option to expand the heap block using realloc safely.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Practice implementing do/while validation loops and safe realloc patterns using a temporary pointer.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Implement a do/while that rejects grades outside 0–100. After initial input ask the user if they want to add more slots; if yes, compute the new size and use realloc via a temporary pointer. Check tmp for NULL before assigning back to grades.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample:
After implementing, run: gcc -std=c11 main.c -o main && printf "2
50
-5
70
n
" | ./main -> Average grade: 60.00
teachingPlaylist.scenario: A data-entry session where more students arrive after the teacher started entering grades and the program must expand storage.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Add the validation loop and realloc flow, compile, and test with an invalid grade and then a successful input.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Assigning realloc result directly to the original pointer and losing the old block if realloc fails.
teachingPlaylist.recap: Always validate input and use a temporary pointer when calling realloc to avoid leaks on failure.
codeSteps: Change the scanf line to a do/while that checks 0 <= grade <= 100.
After the loop add prompt to add more grades and implement realloc using a temp pointer.
Check tmp for NULL before reassigning.
Compile and run the provided example to verify behavior.

teachingPlaylist.title: Verify: Edge-case testing and extension planning
teachingPlaylist.description: Run edge-case tests, confirm memory-safety, and design an extension to store names with grades.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Be able to test for invalid counts, large values, and sketch a safe plan for adding name storage with char**.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Run tests for num_grades zero and invalid input; verify the program prints helpful messages and does not crash. Then outline how you'd add name storage: allocate char** names = calloc(count, sizeof(char*)); for each student allocate a char buffer and free every names[i] before freeing names.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: Run: gcc -std=c11 main.c -o main && printf "0\n" | ./main -> Number of grades must be positive.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: Preparing the app for production where users may send malformed inputs or try edge cases.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Run the provided checks and write down how you'd free names after extending the program to store strings.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Forgetting to free individually allocated strings before freeing the array of pointers.
teachingPlaylist.recap: Test edge cases and free in reverse order of allocation. Plan extensions before coding.
codeSteps: Sketch (on paper) the steps to allocate and free an array of names (char**).
If time remains, implement the names feature.

tasks.title: Scene 1 — Observe & Understand the Starter Program
tasks.narratorGuide: We'll run the provided program so you can observe how a pointer is used to hold a heap allocation and how the program prompts for input. Pay attention to the prompts and the final printed average. Predict what happens to memory when malloc succeeds and when it fails. After running, I'll ask you to explain in your own words which variable holds the address and where the floats live.

tasks.title: Scene 2 — Modify & Experiment: Use calloc and initialize pointer
tasks.narratorGuide: Now we'll make a small focused edit: initialize grades to NULL and use calloc instead of malloc. calloc will zero-initialize the memory (helpful as a safety net). After compiling, run the same inputs and compare results. Predict whether the printed average will change and why. This targeted change reinforces how allocation functions differ and why pointer initialization is good practice.

tasks.title: Scene 3 — Build & Integrate: Allow resizing with realloc and reject invalid grades
tasks.narratorGuide: Now you'll integrate new functionality. First, guard each scanf result: keep prompting until the grade is between 0 and 100. Second, after the initial loop offer the user a chance to add more slots; if they accept, use realloc to increase the heap block and continue reading additional grades. These changes practice safe use of realloc and reinforce the contract: always check realloc's return and avoid losing the original pointer.

tasks.title: Scene 4 — Verify & Extend: Test edge cases and propose an extension
tasks.narratorGuide: In this final scene you'll verify correctness by running several tests: zero or negative counts, invalid grades, and the realloc path. Observe program behavior and memory-safety practices like checking returned pointers and nulling after free. As an extension, sketch how you'd allocate and free an array of char* to store names alongside grades — this pairs pointer-to-pointer thinking with heap management.
